common_name: Harold Epstein Dwarf Fothergilla (Wild-Collected Miniature Witch Alder)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring or fall in moist, acidic, organically rich, well-drained soil in full sun to considerable shade; because this miniature form does not come true from seed, propagate only from cuttings.

directions: This miniature selection descends from an unusually small population of wild dwarf gardenii that plantsman Harold Epstein discovered near Jesup, Georgia, later grown on and distributed through the Arnold Arboretum's plant introduction program. It forms an exceptionally tight, low mound of small, dark green, oval leaves rarely topping two feet, making it the smallest named fothergilla available and well suited to rock gardens or the front of a shaded border. Small, honey-scented white bottlebrush flower spikes open on bare stems in April, followed by a dependable orange-red fall display that holds up even in considerably shadier spots than most fothergillas will tolerate. Give it evenly moist, acidic, humus-rich soil, since its miniature root system has little reserve to buffer against drought.

common_name: Sea Spray Fothergilla (Glaucous Blue-Green Witch Alder)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring or fall in evenly moist, acidic soil with a pH near 5 to 6.5 and mulch over the shallow root zone; site with morning sun and afternoon shade in hot climates.

directions: Sea Spray is a naturally occurring hybrid between mountain witch alder and the coastal dwarf species, prized less for a fiery fall show and more for its cool, glaucous blue-green summer foliage with a waxy, sea-glass sheen on the leaf undersides. Honey-scented white bottlebrush flowers tipped in soft yellow anthers open on bare stems in April before the leaves emerge, drawing in early bees. Still rare in cultivation, it prefers evenly moist, acidic soil and benefits from a mulch layer over its shallow root system, tolerating some drought once established but performing best without extended dry spells. Fall color is more muted than typical fothergillas, shifting to bronze or dark red-brown rather than the multicolor blaze of the species, so site it for its foliage texture and habit rather than autumn fireworks.
sources: Michael Dirr's Manual of Woody Landscape Plants
